reels.title: The notebook you hand over every time

beats.say: Why does a long chat with Claude cost more than a short one, even when your newest question is tiny?

Imagine a helper with no memory. Every time you ask something, you must hand over the whole notebook: everything you said, everything they answered, every document they looked at. They read it all, then reply.
So the notebook grows. Page ten costs more to read than page one. The reading is what you pay for, counted in tokens, which are small chunks of words.
Writing a reply costs extra, because writing is harder than reading. And if the helper has already read the first pages recently, they skim them cheaply.

show.title: Two price tags
items: Reading the notebook: cheaper per word
Writing a reply: costs several times more
Pages seen recently: skimmed at a discount

check.q: Why does the tenth message in a chat cost more to process than the first, even if both are one line?
opts: Later messages are longer
Each turn resends the whole conversation so far
Claude charges more for later turns
Short messages are rounded up
check.why: Claude has no memory between turns, so the full history is sent and read every time. The history grows, so each turn costs more.

work: Notice how long your current session has been before asking a small question.
Start a fresh chat when you switch to an unrelated task.
Avoid pasting big documents unless Claude truly needs them.

reels.title: Where the tokens go each turn

beats.say: A twenty turn session, and your last message was ten words. Why was that turn so expensive?

Because each turn resends everything. Say the system prompt and CLAUDE dot m d are five thousand tokens. On turn two Claude reads a file of ten thousand tokens. From then on, every turn carries those fifteen thousand tokens again.
Input is billed per token sent, every turn. Output is what Claude writes, and it costs several times more per token. Thinking tokens count as output too.
Cache helps. Unchanged early context is read back at a fraction of the price, often about a tenth. But edit something early, and everything after it is paid at full price again.

chip.text: Cache read: about one tenth price
Early change = full price after it

check.q: Your system prompt and a file total 15,000 tokens. You then send 20 short turns. What is the main cost driver?
opts: The words in your short messages
Those 15,000 tokens being sent again on every turn
The number of files on disk
Claude's typing speed
check.why: Short messages are tiny. The big repeated context is resent each turn, so it dominates input cost, though caching reduces its price.

work: Keep CLAUDE.md short and focused, since it rides along on every turn.
Ask for targeted file sections instead of whole large files.
Watch output-heavy requests like full rewrites, since output costs more per token.

reels.title: Cost traps and cache gotchas

beats.say: Why did one pasted log file quietly make the next fifty turns more expensive?
Because anything that enters the conversation stays in it. A thirty thousand token log is resent every turn. Over fifty turns, that is one and a half million input tokens, from one paste.

Cache softens this, but only for a stable prefix. If you edit CLAUDE dot m d, switch model, or change tools mid session, the prefix changes and the cache misses. Cache entries also expire after a few idle minutes, so a long break means a full price restart.

show.title: What breaks the cache
items: Editing early context such as CLAUDE.md
Switching model or tools mid session
Idling past the cache lifetime of a few minutes

beats.say: Two more gotchas. Extended thinking and high effort add output tokens, the expensive kind. And a subagent's work uses tokens too, even if only its summary returns.

check.q: Midway through a long session you edit CLAUDE.md. What is the likely cost effect?
opts: None, cached content is permanent
The cached prefix changes, so later turns may be paid at full input price
Output tokens become free
The session resets and context is cleared
check.why: Caching works on an unchanged prefix. Changing early context invalidates the cache from that point, so the content after it is billed at full price until it is cached again.

work: Summarize or trim big logs before pasting, and paste only the failing section.
Settle CLAUDE.md and model choice at the start of a session, not midway.
Reserve extended thinking and high effort for genuinely hard problems.

reels.title: Spending tokens like an architect

beats.say: You have a big task and a tight budget. Do you just pick the cheapest model?
Not quite. Price per token is only one factor. A cheaper model that needs three retries can cost more than a stronger model that gets it right once. Match the model to the difficulty.

Spend where tokens buy value. Use Haiku for simple lookups, Sonnet for everyday coding, Opus for hard design and tricky bugs. Keep context lean: point to files instead of pasting, and start fresh sessions for new tasks.

chip.text: Pay for strength only when needed

beats.say: Keep the early context stable so the cache keeps paying off. On a subscription, the same tokens drain your limits, so waste means fewer finished tasks by Friday.

show.title: Budget principles
items: Stable early context keeps cache hits high
Wasted tokens shrink your weekly capacity

check.q: A cheap model needs three attempts on a hard bug, each resending a large context. What is the best conclusion?
opts: It is always cheaper, since the rate is lower
Total cost may exceed one pass of a stronger model, so match model to difficulty
Retries are free because of caching
Only output tokens matter
check.why: Cost is rate times tokens used across all attempts. Repeated attempts resend context and add output, so a stronger model that succeeds once can be cheaper overall.

work: Default to Sonnet, and move to Haiku or Opus deliberately for easy or hard tasks.
Start a new session per task and reference files by path instead of pasting.
Track which workflows burn the most usage and trim their context first.

reels.title: Why a long chat costs more

beats.say: Why does a long chat with an AI cost more than a short one, even when your latest question is tiny?

Picture a waiter who forgets everything between sentences. Each time you speak, he rereads the whole conversation from the start, and you pay for every word he reads. Hours of chatter means a very long reread.
Four habits keep the bill small. Start a fresh chat for each new task. Tell the assistant exactly where to look. Don't let it print giant files. And use a smaller, cheaper helper for easy jobs.

check.q: Why does a very long chat make each new question more expensive?
opts: The assistant gets tired and works slower
The whole earlier conversation is re-sent every turn
Longer chats use a more expensive model
check.why: The model has no memory between turns, so the full history is sent again each time and you pay for all of it.

work: Start a fresh chat whenever you switch to an unrelated task.
Notice how long your current session has run before sending the next message.

reels.title: Where the tokens go on each turn

beats.say: Your message is ten words. So why did that turn cost fifty thousand tokens? A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a word.

show.sub: A token is roughly one word

beats.say: Because the model has no memory. Every turn re-sends the whole history: system prompt, project notes, files read, and every earlier reply. Twenty turns at fifty thousand tokens each is a million tokens billed.

Two habits fix it. Slash clear between unrelated tasks, which resets history to almost nothing. When one task runs long, use slash compact, and say what to keep, like the failing test names and the plan.

show.title: Shrink the history
items: Tell compact what to keep: failing tests, the plan

check.q: You finish a bug fix and start an unrelated feature in the same session. What is the best move?
opts: Keep going so the model remembers everything
Run clear, then start the feature
Switch to a bigger model
check.why: Old history is re-sent and billed on every turn. Clearing removes context the new task does not need.

work: Run clear at every task boundary today.
When a task is long, compact with a note naming what must survive.

reels.title: Exploration and noisy output

beats.say: You asked it to fix one bug. Why did it read ten files and print a five megabyte CSV?

show.text: One bug, ten files, one huge CSV

beats.say: Vague requests force exploration. Every file it reads, and every line a command prints, lands in the history and is re-sent on every later turn. A five megabyte file can run past a million tokens.

chip.text: Every printed line is billed again and again

beats.say: So be specific. Point at files with the at sign, give the error and the command, and say where not to look. Quiet the output: pytest dash q dash x, pipe to tail forty, and head twenty on data files.

show.title: Quiet commands
show.text:
pytest -q -x
python3 -m unittest -q
make build | tail -40
head -20 data.csv

beats.say: Don't guess where the window went. Run slash context to see the system prompt, project notes, tools, files and conversation. Slash cost or slash usage shows the spend.

check.q: Which prompt is cheapest and most reliable for a failing test?
opts: Fix the bug
Fix the failure in @orders.py shown by pytest -q -x; do not look in the vendor folder
Read the whole repo and find problems
check.why: It names the file, the error and the command, and limits exploration, so fewer files and less output enter the history.

work: Never let a command print a whole data file; use head or tail.
Run context when a session feels expensive, before changing habits.

reels.title: Choosing the right trade-off

beats.say: Using the biggest model to rename a variable: what are you actually paying for?

show.sub: Paying for reasoning you do not use

beats.say: Wrong model is the cheapest driver to fix. Send routine edits to Haiku or Sonnet, and save Opus for hard reasoning, like a tangled design bug. Switch with slash model.
But every habit has a cost. Clear throws away context you may need to rebuild. Compact is lossy, so name what to keep. Saying where not to look can hide the real cause.

show.title: Habit trade-offs
items: Do not look here: may hide root cause

beats.say: Measure first, with slash cost for API billing or slash usage for subscriptions. And keep project notes and tool lists lean, because they ride along on every single turn.

show.title: Measure and trim
items: Only the MCP tools you need

check.q: What is the main risk of telling the assistant not to look in certain folders?
opts: It costs more tokens
It may miss the real root cause
It forces a bigger model
check.why: Narrowing the search saves tokens, but if the cause lives in the excluded area, you get a confident wrong fix.

work: Default to Sonnet or Haiku and escalate to Opus only when stuck.
Review your project notes and enabled tools for anything that is not used every session.

reels.title: The backpack you pay for every trip

beats.say: Why does Claude use up credits before you type a single word?

show.sub: Something is already in the bag

beats.say: Picture a hiker who carries the same backpack on every trip. Inside are your project notes, and a manual for every tool you have connected. Each trip, you pay for the weight, even if you never open most of it.
So pack light. Keep your notes file short. Leave unused tool manuals at home. Send a helper to search the library, and it brings back one page instead of twenty books.
And ask for short answers. Fewer words out means fewer credits spent.

check.q: In the backpack picture, what does the weight stand for?
opts: Everything loaded into the conversation that you pay for each trip
How smart the answer is
How many files are on your disk
check.why: Notes and tool descriptions ride along in every session, so you pay for them whether or not they are used.

work: Open your CLAUDE.md and mark lines you have never needed.
List which tool plug-ins you connected and which you used this week.

reels.title: What sits in context, and what it costs

beats.say: What actually sits in context before you type anything?

Your CLAUDE.md file loads every session. Each connected MCP server, which is a plug-in offering tools, adds its tool descriptions too. All of it is read again on every turn. Forty precise lines might cost a few hundred tokens. Four hundred vague ones cost roughly ten times that, every single turn.

Searching is the big one. Reading twenty files yourself might dump tens of thousands of tokens into your main context. A subagent reads them in its own context and returns a ten line summary. Your main context grows by a few hundred tokens instead.
Rule of thumb: whatever sits in context, you pay for again each turn.

check.q: Why delegate a twenty file search to a subagent?
opts: The files are read faster
Only a short summary lands in your main context
Subagents are free
check.why: The subagent absorbs the file contents in its own context. Your main context only grows by the summary, so every later turn stays cheaper.

work: Trim CLAUDE.md toward about 40 precise rules.
Run the mcp command and disable servers you did not use this week.
Next time you need a wide search, ask for a subagent and a 10 line summary.

reels.title: Where trimming goes wrong

beats.say: What can go wrong when you trim context too hard?

Disable an MCP server and its tools vanish, so turn it back on with the mcp command when a task needs it. Cut CLAUDE.md too far and Claude loses rules it needed, so shorten by being precise, not by deleting.
A subagent summary is lossy. It may skip the one line you needed. Ask it to return file names and line numbers, so you can check the source yourself.

chip.text: Ask for file and line refs

beats.say: Asking for less has a limit too. Five lines is great for a command, and risky for a debugging explanation you must understand.

check.q: How do you reduce the risk of a lossy subagent summary?
opts: Ask for a longer summary of everything
Ask it to include file names and line numbers
Stop using subagents
check.why: References let you jump to the source and verify the one detail the summary may have dropped, while the summary stays short.

work: Add file and line references to your standard subagent request.
Keep a note of which MCP servers you disabled so you can re-enable them quickly.

reels.title: Fencing in a headless run

beats.say: How do you stop an automated Claude run from burning money while nobody watches?

Headless means running Claude from a script with no human in the chat. Set max turns to cap the number of steps. Set max budget in dollars to cap spending. Restrict the tools so the run cannot wander into the file system or the web.
A grader is the extreme example. No tools, a small model, and a JSON schema forcing a short structured answer. One grade costs about a tenth of a cent, instead of twenty-five cents.
Same task, about two hundred and fifty times cheaper, because every freedom was removed.

show.sub: Remove freedoms you do not need

check.q: A headless run hits max turns midway. What is the likely result?
opts: It finishes the work anyway
It stops with partial work, so your script must handle that
It switches to a bigger model
check.why: Limits are hard stops. Scripts should expect incomplete output and either retry with care or flag it for a human.

work: Add max-turns and max-budget-usd to every scheduled Claude script.
Give each script only the tools it truly needs.
Handle the limit-reached case in your script rather than assuming success.

reels.title: Saving credits is not the goal

beats.say: When is saving credits the wrong goal?
Savings have a price. A tiny model with no tools is perfect for grading, and wrong for a hard refactor, where one failed attempt costs more than a good first one.
Delegating to subagents adds overhead and loses detail, so use it for wide searches, not for a three line fix. Many MCP servers are worth it only if you use them weekly.

show.title: Use each lever where it pays
items: Keep MCP servers you use weekly

beats.say: Choose by cost of a mistake. Constrain hard for high volume, low risk jobs. Give room for rare, high stakes ones. And measure cost per finished task, not per message.

check.q: Which job best suits a no-tools, small-model, schema-bound run?
opts: A large multi-file refactor
High-volume grading of short answers
An open-ended incident investigation
check.why: Grading is repetitive, low risk and well defined, so tight constraints cut cost sharply without hurting quality.

work: Sort your Claude jobs into high-volume low-risk and rare high-stakes, and set limits for each.
Track cost per completed task for one week before changing anything else.

reels.title: Cheap is not the same as saving

beats.say: Is the cheapest option always the one that saves you money?
Imagine hiring a builder. One quotes less because he skips the final inspection. The house goes up cheaper. Then the roof leaks, and you pay to tear it open and fix it.
Using an AI assistant works the same way. It charges in credits, which are small units of usage. Skipping the test run saves a few credits. But a hidden bug costs far more to find later.
So judge cost per correct result, not cost per message. Trim real waste, like repeating old chat, wandering around, and giant outputs. Never trim the checking.

check.q: A teammate skips running tests to save credits. What is the main problem?
opts: Tests cost more than they save, always
A bug found later can cost far more than the credits saved
Credits are only spent on tests
It makes the assistant slower to answer
check.why: The goal is cost per correct result. Skipping verification saves little now but moves a larger cost to later rework.

work: Next time you ask an assistant for a change, ask it to run the tests too.
Notice which of your habits are real waste, like pasting huge files, and which are checking.

reels.title: Cost per correct result, with numbers

beats.say: Which is cheaper: a three thousand token try, or a five thousand token try?
Say a quick prompt, just fix it, costs three thousand tokens and works one time in three. You need about three tries for one good result. That is nine thousand tokens per correct result.
Now ask for a plan first, then a test run. It costs five thousand tokens but works nine times in ten. Divide five thousand by point nine. About five thousand six hundred per correct result.
So the formula is tokens spent, divided by success rate. A pricier try can be the cheaper path.

check.q: Option A costs 2,000 tokens a try and succeeds 1 time in 4. Option B costs 4,000 tokens and succeeds 4 times in 5. Which has the lower cost per correct result?
opts: A, at 8,000 tokens
B, at 5,000 tokens
They are equal
A, because each try is cheaper
check.why: A is 2,000 divided by 0.25, which is 8,000. B is 4,000 divided by 0.8, which is 5,000. Success rate matters as much as price per try.

work: Estimate your own success rate on a common task, then compute tokens per correct result.
Add a plan step and a test run to prompts for changes where mistakes are expensive.

reels.title: Which waste to cut, and what to keep

beats.say: Your bill is high. Which part do you cut first?

Cut waste. A long chat is reread on every message, so start fresh when the topic changes. Letting the assistant wander through the whole codebase burns tokens on files that never matter. Pasting a ten thousand line log does the same.
The wrong model is waste in both directions. A top model renaming a variable is overkill. A small model on a tricky design fails, and you pay for every retry.
But never cut verification. Skipping tests looks free on the bill. The cost just moves to a production bug, where it is far bigger.

check.q: Which change is safe to make to cut your assistant bill?
opts: Skip the test run on small changes
Start a fresh chat when the topic changes
Use the smallest model for every task
Ask for no plan to save tokens
check.why: Old history is reread every message, so a fresh chat removes pure waste. The others cut verification or risk failed retries.

work: Start a new session when you switch tasks instead of carrying a long history.
Ask for filtered or summarized output rather than full logs.
Pick the model by task difficulty, and keep the test step always.

reels.title: Spend by risk, measure what merges

beats.say: A token costs fractions of a cent. An engineer hour costs real money. So what are you actually optimizing?

Count the whole cost of a change: tokens, retries, review time, and incidents. Engineer time usually dwarfs the token bill, so an extra plan step that saves one review loop pays for itself many times.
Match rigor to risk. A payment migration gets a strong model, a written plan, and full tests. A throwaway script gets a small model and a quick look.
Track cost per merged change that passes. If you only track tokens, you will drift toward cheap and wrong.

check.q: Which metric best steers a team toward efficient assistant use?
opts: Total tokens used per week
Tokens per message
Cost per merged change that passes its tests
Number of prompts sent
check.why: It includes retries, review time and quality. Raw token counts reward cheap but wrong output.

work: Define risk tiers and set the model and verification level for each.
Report cost per merged passing change, including review time, not just the token bill.
Skip heavy planning only for throwaway work where a mistake is cheap.
